abstract.text:
Abstract—This work presents a three-phase unbalanced contin-
uation power ﬂow algorithm for voltage stability assessment of
distribution systems with high penetration of distributed energy
resources (DERs). Analyzing distribution system voltage stability
with DER will allow high penetration of renewable energy nec-
essary for the sustainability goals. The developed algorithm can
analyze voltage stability for both the meshed and radial systems
and the balanced and unbalanced three-phase distribution sys-
tems. The developed tool allows the voltage stability analysis to
facilitate the planning, operation, control, and distribution system
management. The impact of DER on the voltage stability of several
test cases has been analyzed considering constant power ( PQ )
and regulated-voltage ( PV ) modes of operation for DER units.
Moreover, different voltage stability case studies are presented to
demonstrate the impact of unbalance, load increment, and network
topology on the maximum loading capacity. Results using the IEEE
13-node feeder, the 18-bus balanced shipboard system, the 13-node
CIGRE benchmark system, and the 136-bus redial distribution
feeder demonstrate that the developed continuation power ﬂow
tool can efﬁciently perform voltage stability analysis for active
distribution systems.

system in a reliable and efﬁcient mode considering the
continuous growth in demand driven by environmental, eco-
nomic, and technical constraints. V oltage collapse has been
one of the prime reasons for several signiﬁcant disturbances

in the past [1], [2], and as a result, voltage stability assessment
research has received great attention [3]–[5]. V oltage stability is
usually considered a local phenomenon, but the impacts could be
widespread and could lead to a system-level voltage collapse [6].
V oltage stability of power systems has been a vastly studied
topic for transmission system analysis [7], [8]. The continuation
power ﬂow (CPF) method has always been considered one of
the best methods to evaluate voltage stability [9]–[11]. CPF-
based approaches have proven their mettle and have become
a necessary tool in many energy control centers. Transmission
system operators use CPF to determine the maximum loading
capacity and also for detailed contingency analysis. In gen-
eral, the CPF-based approaches use predictor–corrector steps
to trace the P –V curves as the loading multiplier is increased
from the base case till the collapse point. As the system be-
comes stressed, the power ﬂow Jacobian approaches singularity,
and CPF uses parameterization and augmentation of power
ﬂow Jacobian to ensure convergence under stressed operating
conditions.
CPF for distribution networks has received relatively less
attention compared to transmission. Most mature transmission
analysis tools have well-developed CPF libraries capable of
tracing the static voltage behavior. Some researchers have tried
extending the conventional forward–backward sweep power
ﬂow to develop CPF tools for distribution [12]. The major
disadvantage of forward–backward sweep-based CPF is limited
applicability in the analysis of meshed distribution networks.
In [13], Ju et al. have presented a loop-based CPF method for
distribution systems, but this algorithm can only be used for
radial and weakly meshed networks. In [14], Sheng and Chi-
ang have developed a comprehensive three-phase continuation
power ﬂow (TPCPF) tool for distribution networks. The tool
developed in [14] uses a modiﬁed Newton method for corrector
implementation. Dou [15] also consider the traditional Newton
method for the development of the CPF tool for distribution
networks with high distributed energy resource (DER) pene-
tration. The Newton method in its traditional form has faced
convergence issues in the power ﬂow analysis of distribution
networks due to their appreciably high R/X ratio. Thus, a CPF
tool embedded with a power ﬂow solution method suitable for
meshed and radial distribution networks is highly desirable to
suit modern active distribution systems’ planning and opera-
tional analysis needs.

Traditional power ﬂow methods adopted for transmission
system analysis have faced convergence issues when applied to
analyze the distribution system. The reason behind unsuitability
lies in the special characteristics of distribution networks. The
distribution networks possess a comparatively high R/X ratio
and are mostly radial in the literature. That, coupled with the
multiphase unbalanced operation and increasing penetration of
DERs, has resulted in numerical issues when the traditional
Newton method is used for distribution networks [16], [17].
The convergence issues are further aggravated by distribution
systems moving toward more meshed topologies. This evolving
active nature of distribution networks necessitates dedicated
power ﬂow algorithms for unbalanced distribution system anal-
ysis. The three-phase power ﬂow methods explained in [18] and
[19] use the current injection method for power ﬂow analysis in
distribution networks. Recent modernization of the electric grid
with smart grid revolution has made tremendous modiﬁcations
in distribution systems’ structure. A high degree of unbalance,
DER penetration, and multiphase radial feeders make voltage
stability a pivotal concern in distribution networks. The three-
phase current injection method (TCIM) in [19] is a powerful dis-
tribution power ﬂow solver for both meshed and radial networks.
This method has also been adopted in commercial-grade distri-
bution solvers such as OPENDSS [20] and GRIDLAB-D [21].
OPENDSS [20] uses a TCIM for analysis of both radial and
meshed distribution networks, whereas GRIDLAB-D [20] uses
forward–backward sweep for analysis of radial conﬁgurations
and uses the current injection method for meshed conﬁgurations.
Because of the superior performance of the current injection
method in three-phase distribution analyses, this work considers
using the TCIM [18], [19] for the development of the proposed
CPF tool for active distribution networks.
This work builds on our previous work [22] and presents the
TPCPF tool for voltage stability analysis with the following
contributions.
1) Developed formulation and algorithm for CPF for un-
balanced three-phase distribution power systems with
DERs using the current injection power ﬂow method, the
adaptive step predictor–corrector, thePV –PQ switching
algorithm, and the nose point convergence criterion.
2) Investigated the effect of DERs in improving the voltage
proﬁles and improving the system loading margin. The
impact of unbalance, topology, DER penetration, and DER
models is also demonstrated on the system loading margin.
3) Analyzed the performance for both meshed and radial
active distribution networks.
4) V alidated the performance for four test cases: IEEE 13-
node feeder, 18-bus balanced shipboard system, 13-node
CIGRE benchmark system, and 136-bus redial distribu-
tion feeder.

conclusion.text:
V. C ONCLUSION
This work describes development of a three-phase unbalanced
CPF algorithm for active distribution systems using the TCIM,
adaptive step predictor–corrector,PV –PQ switching, and nose
point convergence criteria. The TCIM allows incorporating
DERs using a PV (voltage-regulated) or PQ (constant-power)
model. This tool can be utilized for the voltage stability assess-
ment of unbalanced distribution feeders with high penetration
of DERs. The impacts of load increment on the system for
both (balanced and unbalanced) radial and meshed distribution
networks have been investigated. PV and PQ models for the
DGs have been studied, and their signiﬁcance is presented with
numerical results. Thus,P –V curves obtained using the TPCPF
tool can help determine the weakest system bus and provide a
guideline for the optimum placement of the distributed genera-
tion to improve the voltage stability of the system. The developed
TPCPF tool has been validated for multiple test systems, in-
cluding the IEEE 13-node feeder, the 18-bus balanced shipboard
system, the 13-node CIGRE benchmark system, and the 136-bus
